        booking -> pricing "uses" "HTTP"
        mobile -> dispatch "Requests dispatch via" "gRPC"
        fleet -> scheduler "Registers nightly tasks in" "gRPC"
        pricing -> rates "Looks up rules in" "in-process"
        contracts -> payments "Charges cards through" "REST/JSON"
        damage -> mediadb "Stores damage photos in" "SQL"
        reports -> fleetdb "Reads booking records from" "SQL"
        maintenance -> fleetdb "Stores service records in" "SQL"
        search -> fleetdb "Reads availability from" "SQL"

The model parses and validates cleanly (no syntax errors), so everything below is about C4 modeling quality, not well-formedness. I reviewed it read-only — nothing on disk was changed. I confirmed the structure with the Structurizr inspector/parser, which independently flagged several of these.

## Elements

- **`rates` (Pricing Rules Library)** — Modeled as a `container`, but a shared code library is not a deployable unit, which is what a C4 container is. The `pricing -> rates` edge is even labeled "in-process," confirming it's linked into the Pricing Service rather than a separate deployable. It shouldn't be a box in a container diagram; it's an implementation detail of the Pricing Service.

- **`payments` (Payment Provider)** — Modeled as a generic `element` rather than a `softwareSystem`, and not tagged external. An external system like a payment provider should be a software system in C4; a bare element loses that meaning and isn't rendered as an external-system boundary.

- **`telemetryFeed` (Vehicle Telemetry Feed)** — Also a generic `element` rather than a `softwareSystem`. It is tagged external (better than `payments`), but the element type is still wrong for an external telemetry source.

- **`legacy` (Legacy Billing System)** — Disconnected: no relationships to/from anything and present on no view (inspector-confirmed). It's also described as "the retired billing system being phased out," so its presence is questionable. Either connect it (showing how Fleet Manager still interacts with it during the phase-out) or remove it.

- **`scheduler` (Batch Scheduler)** — Described as "runs the nightly pricing and maintenance batch," but the only edge touching it is `fleet -> scheduler`. There are no `scheduler -> pricing` or `scheduler -> maintenance` edges, so the model doesn't show the batch it claims to run. Description and relationships are inconsistent.

- **`dispatch` (Dispatch Service)** — Described as "assigns vehicles to bookings," but it has only an incoming edge (`mobile -> dispatch`) and no outgoing edge to the booking or fleet containers. It's a dead end that doesn't complete the story its description implies.

- **`notifications`, `damage`, `reports`, `search`, `contracts`, `maintenance`** — Each is a dead end with no incoming relationship, even though its description implies one: notifications "sends … messages" (to whom?), damage "records … damage" (who feeds it?), reports "produces … reports" (who triggers/consumes it?), search "finds vehicles" (who queries it?), contracts "manages rental contracts" (who creates them?), maintenance "plans servicing" (who triggers it — presumably the scheduler, which has no edge to it). The model doesn't show what drives these containers.

## Relationships

- **`booking -> pricing` "uses"** — The description "uses" is too vague to be useful. Every other relationship uses a meaningful verb phrase ("Reserves vehicles in," "Charges cards through"); this one should too (e.g., "Requests a price quote from").

- **`queue -> notifications` "Delivers booking events to"** — The queue is described as carrying "fleet events," but this edge says it delivers "booking events," and no element publishes booking events to the queue (only `telemetry -> queue` does). The queue's contents are inconsistent with its description and have no source.

## Views & workspace

- **Container view** — Has no explicit key or name, so Structurizr auto-generated `Container-001` / "Container View: Fleet Manager" (inspector-confirmed). Auto-generated keys aren't stable over time and can break references; give it an explicit key and a description, like the system context view has.

- **Workspace** — No scope is declared. The inspector recommends `SoftwareSystem` or `Landscape`; since this model is about one system and its context, `SoftwareSystem` is the right scope.

- **System context view "CustomerContext"** — Named and described as showing "the customer's journey around the system," but it actually includes the Payment Provider and Vehicle Telemetry Feed, which aren't part of the customer's journey. The name/description don't match the content — it's really a general system context view.

- **`manager` (Fleet Manager software system)** — The inspector notes it has containers but no attached documentation or architecture decisions. Attaching at least the key decisions would make it more useful as an architecture document. (Softer, tool-driven point.)

The two most consequential issues are the **`rates` library masquerading as a container** (it misrepresents the deployment architecture) and the **cluster of dead-end containers plus the disconnected `legacy` system** (the model is incomplete and internally inconsistent — several elements describe interactions the relationships never show).
